scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Original C1 assessment draft testing qualified argument, structural inequality and the value of unmeasured learning.

tabs.title: Argument and Evidence
tabs.description: Examine the structure and logic of the argument.

tabs.title: Implications
tabs.description: Apply the reasoning to educational choices.

questions.q: What is the author's main reservation about encouraging students to embrace every challenge?
choices: The message is too difficult for younger learners to remember.
It makes successful students less interested in higher marks.
The message can suggest that obstacles are always a matter of individual effort.
It prevents teachers from giving detailed practical feedback.
questions.explanation: Paragraph one criticises the individualising implication of improvement slogans, not the general value of resilience.

questions.q: What is the central weakness of advising both students simply to 'try harder'?
choices: It gives the students too much freedom to choose their methods.
It ignores unequal opportunities to act on that advice.
It assumes that the two students received different marks.
It asks both students to use the same school textbook.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two contrasts equal results with unequal material support and distinguishes useful strategies from access to resources.

questions.q: What does the phrase 'curiosity risks becoming another obligation' imply?
choices: Students no longer want to discuss ideas with their friends.
Curiosity becomes valuable only when linked to a career.
Every leisure activity should be included in the school timetable.
Learners may begin judging even enjoyable exploration by productivity.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three argues that exploration, debate and leisure can have value even when no progress indicator records it.

questions.q: Why does the writer make the two students' assessment results equally poor?
choices: To isolate differences in resources rather than the marks themselves.
To prove that their knowledge and effort were identical.
To argue that no assessment can ever measure learning.
To suggest that both students should receive the same advice.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two contrasts equal results with unequal material support and distinguishes useful strategies from access to resources.

questions.q: What is the point of saying that advice cannot create a quiet room or an extra hour?
choices: Teachers should stop suggesting better learning strategies.
Only students with private study rooms can improve.
Strategies can be helpful without removing material constraints.
Homework should never be assigned to disadvantaged students.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two contrasts equal results with unequal material support and distinguishes useful strategies from access to resources.

questions.q: What role does the example of a debate without agreement play?
choices: It shows how learning may be valuable without a measurable result.
It demonstrates why debates should replace written examinations.
It shows that reaching agreement is usually undesirable.
It suggests students should avoid receiving feedback on debates.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three argues that exploration, debate and leisure can have value even when no progress indicator records it.

questions.q: How does the final paragraph qualify its call for greater school responsibility?
choices: Student effort is unnecessary when support is provided.
Students still have an active role in examining their work.
Responsibility belongs entirely to the student's family.
Schools should allow students to choose their own grades.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four retains student responsibility while also calling for more concrete support from schools.

questions.q: A school gives motivational posters but no quiet place for study. Which improvement best reflects the article?
choices: Replace all tests with student self-evaluations.
Ask teachers to reward enthusiasm instead of attainment.
Tell students to spend more leisure time studying.
Provide supervised study facilities as well as encouragement.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four retains student responsibility while also calling for more concrete support from schools.

questions.q: A pupil reads widely for pleasure but cannot show a rising score. How would the author most likely assess that activity?
choices: It should be stopped until examination results improve.
It may have educational value beyond the score that is measured.
Its value depends on how quickly the pupil finishes each book.
It is only useful if the pupil writes a formal book review.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three argues that exploration, debate and leisure can have value even when no progress indicator records it.

questions.q: Which policy best combines personal agency with institutional responsibility?
choices: Promise every learner an improved grade after additional effort.
Assume the same advice is fair whenever grades are the same.
Measure all learning activities so that effort is always visible.
Offer specific feedback, access to support and opportunities to revise.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four retains student responsibility while also calling for more concrete support from schools.
